title: Signal Chat Contempt: Senior US Officials Mock European Allies in Leaked War Planning Thread
description_short: Signal Chat Contempt: Senior US Officials Mock European Allies in Leaked War Planning Thread
description_medium: In March 2025, a Signal group chat among top US security officials — including National Security Adviser Michael Waltz, Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — was accidentally exposed when Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg was added to the thread.
description_long:
In March 2025, a Signal group chat among top US security officials — including National Security Adviser Michael Waltz, Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — was accidentally exposed when Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg was added to the thread. Beyond the classified Houthi strike details, European allies were horrified by the conversation's explicit contempt: Vance complained about European freeloading, Waltz lamented Europe's weak naval forces, and Miller argued that if the US restored freedom of navigation at great cost there needs to be some further gain extracted in return. An EU official told the BBC officials were sick to their stomach. The leak came days after Vance had scandalized European leaders at the Munich Security Conference by calling their political values the enemy within.

The leak exposed private attitudes as well as operational discussion. European officials criticized the remarks, but comments in the chat were not a formal decision to end U.S. security commitments to allies.

title: Trump Promises 'Largest Deportation Operation in American History'
description_short: Trump Promises 'Largest Deportation Operation in American History'
description_medium: Throughout the 2024 campaign, Trump repeatedly promised to launch what he called the 'largest deportation operation in American history' if elected, targeting millions of undocumented immigrants. The plan involved invoking the Alien Enemies Act of 1798, building mass detention camps, and deploying the military for domestic enforcement operations. Immigration experts warned the proposal would cost hundreds of billions of dollars, separate hundreds of thousands of American citizen children from their parents, and require unprecedented violations of due process. Human rights organizations labeled the plan a humanitarian catastrophe in waiting.

title: Trump: DOJ purges national security lawyers
description_short: Trump: DOJ purges national security lawyers
description_medium: On March 8, 2025, the Justice Department removed senior officials working in national security and professional oversight. Among those removed were National Security Division officials Melissa MacTough and Brad Wiegmann, along with leaders in professional-responsibility review, organized-crime enforcement and the U.S. Trustee Program. Former personnel raised concerns about the loss of experience and institutional expertise.
description_long: On March 8, 2025, senior Justice Department officials were removed from roles in national security and professional oversight. The officials included Melissa MacTough and Brad Wiegmann, deputy assistant attorneys general in the National Security Division. MacTough led its intelligence office; Wiegmann oversaw law and policy. Jeffrey Ragsdale at the Office of Professional Responsibility, Adam Cohen at the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces, and Tara Twomey at the Executive Office for U.S. Trustees were also identified among those affected. The positions covered different oversight and enforcement functions, so the departures extended beyond one investigative team. Former officials described the loss of experienced staff as damaging. Cohen said he had served through five presidents and 11 attorneys general without his politics previously being relevant. The department did not give a complete public justification for each removal, and no specific investigative failure was tied to the changes.

title: Trump admin closes DHS / ICE oversight offices
description_short: Trump admin closes DHS / ICE oversight offices
description_medium: On May 23, 2025, employees of three DHS oversight offices were suspended and given separation dates. The offices handled civil rights, immigration-service complaints and detention oversight. DHS characterized the changes as reform, while former personnel questioned whether the remaining staffing could provide meaningful oversight. The suspensions and separation dates sharply reduced staffing, but Congress did not repeal the offices.
description_long: On May 23, 2025, the Trump administration suspended employees and issued separation dates at three Department of Homeland Security oversight offices: Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, the Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman, and the Immigration Detention Ombudsman. The personnel measures disrupted the offices’ work. DHS defended its approach as reform aimed at mismanagement and overlapping responsibilities. CNN reported that staffing was extremely limited during the transition and that officials discussed a small detention-ombudsman team. Former office leader Michelle Brané questioned whether such staffing could meet oversight needs as detention expanded. A budget request also provided no funding for that office. The staff reductions, funding proposal and statutory duties were separate matters. Together they weakened DHS mechanisms for complaints and scrutiny, but do not establish that every later detention problem resulted from these removals. The offices handled civil-rights complaints, immigration-service problems and detention concerns.

title: Trump: Russia infiltrates Antifa groups in Germany to ignite far-right
description_short: Trump: Russia infiltrates Antifa groups in Germany to ignite far-right
description_medium: Suspected Russian influence activity involved websites presenting themselves as German anti-fascist groups. Sites associated with Antifa West Berlin and Antifa Nord Ost promoted an anti-AfD rally in Berlin and showed technical links to infrastructure used by Russian hackers in the 2016 U.S. election. The sites targeted German political audiences.
description_long:
The linked account describes suspected Russian influence activity involving websites presenting themselves as German anti-fascist groups. It cites reporting that sites associated with Antifa West Berlin and Antifa Nord Ost promoted an anti-AfD rally in Berlin while displaying technical connections to infrastructure used by Russian hackers in the 2016 United States election.

One cited connection was a shared server; another involved an anonymized registration email also used for Russian spearphishing sites. Russian media also supported Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany party. Analysts saw the combination as an effort to deepen political division rather than consistently support one ideology.

The websites and technical links raised questions about online impersonation and amplification. They did not show that every anti-fascist group was controlled by Russia or that rally attendees were affiliated with Russian operators. The comparison with U.S. influence activity illustrates how operations can exploit competing political constituencies to deepen division.

description_long:
In a September 2021 interview with podcaster Jack Murphy, J.D. Vance advocated taking control of federal institutions and turning them against the left. His remarks included support for replacing midlevel bureaucrats with political allies if Donald Trump returned to office. The interview predated Project 2025 but expressed a related vision of using executive power to reshape the federal workforce.

Vance also discussed ideas associated with writer Curtis Yarvin, who has argued for concentrated executive control. The event documents a proposed political staffing strategy before Vance became Trump's running mate. title: Trump taps bank, Wall Street regulators for top posts
description_short: Trump taps bank, Wall Street regulators for top posts
description_medium: Donald Trump announced several financial-regulatory nominations on February 11, 2025. Jonathan McKernan was selected to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Jonathan Gould to head the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and Brian Quintenz to lead the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The selections involved agencies overseeing consumer finance, banking, and derivatives markets.
description_long:
Donald Trump announced several financial-regulatory nominations on February 11, 2025. Jonathan McKernan was selected to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Jonathan Gould to head the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and Brian Quintenz to lead the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The selections involved agencies overseeing consumer finance, banking, and derivatives markets.

Trump also nominated John Hurley for a Treasury role overseeing terrorism and financial crimes and Brian Morrissey as Treasury general counsel. McKernan had served on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation board; Gould was a Jones Day partner; Quintenz led policy for Andreessen Horowitz's cryptocurrency business. These backgrounds help explain the regulatory interests involved.

The nominations occurred amid efforts to curtail the CFPB's operations and growing attention to cryptocurrency oversight. Senator Elizabeth Warren questioned the relevance of a leadership nomination if the administration was simultaneously dismantling the agency. These were nominations, not confirmations; the selections did not by themselves place the nominees in office.

title: Donald Trump gives first campaign speech, says he's not running
description_short: Donald Trump gives first campaign speech, says he's not running
description_medium: In October 1987, Donald Trump spoke at a Portsmouth Rotary Club luncheon in New Hampshire as supporters explored whether he might run for president. The event drew a larger audience than appearances by several declared Republican candidates. Trump opened by saying he was not interested in becoming a candidate, while delivering remarks on foreign policy and U.S. leadership. People outside the luncheon held signs urging him to run.
description_long: Donald Trump spoke to the Portsmouth Rotary Club in New Hampshire in October 1987 during early public discussion of a possible presidential campaign. Organizer Michael Dunbar had promoted a draft-Trump effort and arranged the luncheon. The event drew an audience larger than those for appearances by several declared Republican candidates, including Bob Dole, Jack Kemp, and Pat Robertson. Trump began by saying he was not interested in running, but used the speech to discuss national leadership and foreign policy. He criticized U.S. financial support for allies, argued that other countries should pay more, and called for force against Iran. Outside, college students displayed signs encouraging him to seek the presidency. The combination of a campaign-like setting, policy remarks, and explicit denial of candidacy made the appearance newsworthy. It was not a formal campaign launch; it showed Trump testing ideas and attracting attention years before entering electoral politics. Accounts differ on the speech date, placing it on either October 22 or October 23.

title: Trump: WikiLeaks drops over 20,000 DNC emails obtained by Russian hackers
description_short: Trump: WikiLeaks drops over 20,000 DNC emails obtained by Russian hackers
description_medium: WikiLeaks published nearly 20,000 Democratic National Committee emails on July 22, 2016, three days before the party's convention. The stolen messages included discussions of Bernie Sanders, donor perks and communications with journalists. Their release intensified conflict within the Democratic Party as it prepared to nominate Hillary Clinton.
description_long: On July 22, 2016, WikiLeaks released nearly 20,000 emails stolen from the Democratic National Committee, three days before the party's convention. The messages included internal discussion of Senator Bernie Sanders, benefits offered to donors attending the convention and exchanges with journalists. The publication intensified divisions during the Democratic presidential nomination fight. DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz resigned as the convention opened, and the release prompted protests by Sanders supporters. U.S. intelligence agencies later attributed the theft to Russian hackers. The timing and content gave the material a major role in the campaign's public debate, while the breach itself was part of Russia's effort to interfere in the 2016 election. Trump campaign official Rick Gates later said the disclosures diverted attention from unfavorable coverage of Trump, but that retrospective assessment does not show that his campaign arranged the hack. The hack, publication and domestic political response were connected, but the disclosures do not establish that Trump’s campaign arranged the intrusion.
